mcqs.question: In the code sample, what's the actual trade-off of using BaseNotifier (abstract class) instead of the Notifier interface alone?
options: It gives EmailNotifier and SmsNotifier shared logging and a template method for free, at the cost of using up their one supertype slot
It removes the need to ever implement deliver()
It makes send() run faster than the interface version
It prevents EmailNotifier from also implementing other interfaces
mcqs.explanation: The abstract class supplies real shared code (log, the send template) but claims the implementer's single extends slot. deliver() is still required, there's no inherent speed difference, and EmailNotifier can still implement other interfaces alongside extending BaseNotifier.

mcqs.question: Per the compare table, what's the sharpest way to decide between an interface and an abstract class?
options: Always default to an interface, since it's strictly safer in every case
Pick whichever one the language lists first in its documentation
Use an abstract class whenever there are more than two implementers
Count how much implementation is genuinely identical across every implementer — the more there is, the more an abstract class's single-inheritance cost is worth paying
mcqs.explanation: The decision hinges on shared implementation, not implementer count or a blanket default. An interface is 'safer' only when there's nothing real to share; once there's genuine common code, an abstract class's cost becomes worthwhile.

mcqs.question: You initially chose an abstract class, but now need an implementer that already extends something else. What's the easier migration path?
options: There is no way to fix this without rewriting every implementer from scratch
Convert every existing subclass to also extend a second abstract class
Extract the abstract methods into a new interface, have the abstract class implement it, so new code can depend on the interface while old code keeps working
Delete the abstract class and inline its logic into every implementer
mcqs.explanation: Extracting an interface from the abstract class lets new implementers use the interface alone while existing subclasses keep working unchanged. Languages don't allow extending two classes, and neither a full rewrite nor inlining is necessary.

mcqs.question: Why does saying "interfaces are 100% abstract, abstract classes can have implementation" lose points today?
options: Because abstract classes were removed in modern Java versions
Because Java 8's default methods let interfaces carry real method bodies, so the absolute statement is outdated — the sharper line is shared state vs. shared stateless behavior
Because interfaces can now have private instance fields just like abstract classes
Because the statement was never true in any Java version
mcqs.explanation: Default methods (Java 8+) mean interfaces can carry real behavior, so "100% abstract" is stale. Interfaces still can't hold instance fields, abstract classes weren't removed, and the statement was accurate pre-Java 8 — it's just outdated now.
